name: Pigeonhole principle PHP(n) (SAT-natural known-result benchmark)
statement: PHP(n): n pigeons cannot be placed into n-1 holes such that no hole contains two pigeons. Encoded as a CNF formula, PHP(n) is unsatisfiable for every n >= 1.
domain: positive integers n (number of pigeons); encoded over n*(n-1) Boolean variables
quantifiers: universal over placements; the CNF is UNSAT for every n (a theorem, not a conjecture)
status: solved / known result. Included as a known-result benchmark (not an open conjecture) to validate the SAT encoding, DPLL search backend, and independent brute-force UNSAT verifier. PHP(n) is also the classical example of a CNF family requiring exponential-size resolution refutations (Haken, 1985), which is why it is a standard SAT-solver stress test.
known_bounds: proved for all n by a simple counting argument; this framework's brute-force verifier is capacity-limited to small n (see PigeonholeVerifier::kMaxBruteForcePigeons) since it checks UNSAT by exhaustively enumerating all 2^(n*(n-1)) assignments rather than checking a resolution/DRAT proof
certificate_type: candidate_proof / verified_proof: pigeon count n, plus a hash of the exact CNF that was solved
search_backend: custom DPLL SAT solver with unit propagation (src/sat/dpll_solver.cpp)
verification_backend: independent: CNF is rebuilt from n alone (not trusted from the certificate), checked against closed-form variable/clause count invariants, hash-compared against the certificate, then exhaustively brute-forced for a satisfying assignment; this deliberately does not call the DPLL solver at all
references: A. Haken, 'The intractability of resolution', Theoretical Computer Science 39 (1985), 297-308.
This is a standard textbook combinatorics/proof-complexity example; see any introductory proof complexity or SAT solving reference.
